title: This ’34 Ford Pickup Was Built in a Year, but It Wasn’t Finished for Several More

body_markdown:
This summer, Ross Kitman brought his ’34 Ford pickup from his home in Tremonton, Utah, about 80 miles north of Salt Lake City, to the Bonneville Salt Flats, as he has for the past 11 years. We finally ran into him at the[Speed Week](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/gallery-bonneville-speed-week-2026/) car show and got an up-close look at his custom creation.


He bought the truck project in the middle of winter 12 years ago after the previous owner lost interest. It wasn’t much—just a cab, a bed, and a chassis. The previous owner had started work on modifying the frame rails and had also begun stripping the paint off the body. Ross planned on keeping as much of the original patina as possible, so he was glad that he wasn’t starting with so much bare metal. Still, it wasn’t much of a concern. Ross’s day job involves fabricating, wiring, upholstering, and painting horse trailers, so he was plenty familiar with the skills needed to get the pile of parts working and on the road in under a year.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Even with several inches of ice on his driveway, he dove right into the pickup project. Just four days after he’d purchased his new project, Ross had already chopped the roof five inches. But after lowering the roof, he felt that the proportions were off. “It didn’t look right, so I cut the floor out of it,” Ross explained. By refitting the floor and transmission tunnel four inches higher, Ross was able to channel the body over the frame. One thing led to another, and the truck’s lowered stance made the original long bed stick out like a sore thumb. “I cut it down into six pieces, and made it a short bed,” he said.


Next came the chassis. Ross kept many of the parts he got when he bought the project, including the[Ford Model A](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/your-handy-1928-31-ford-model-a-buyers-guide/) axle and transverse spring up front. The backing plates and drum brakes came from a ’53 Ford F100, and a[1976 F-100](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/f~100/1976/1976-ford-f~100-1!!2_ton?id=aCn1I000000CzxbSAC) donated its 9-inch rear axle. “The steering box is unique,” Ross said. It’s from a 1968 Mustang. “Instead of crossover steering, I converted it to push-pull.”


The checkerboard firewall is an homage to vintage hot rods and customs. Ross built a gantry to lift the cab off the chassis and spent three days sitting on top of the engine painting the firewall black, masking a 1.5-inch grid, removing every other square, and painting them antique white. Then everything was unmasked and sprayed with a light mist of pearlescent clearcoat.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Sitting prominently up front, without a hood or hood sides to shroud it, is a[Mopar 440 big-block](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/the-71-cuda-marked-the-end-of-an-era-and-collectors-still-want-in/) . “I pulled the motor and transmission out of a ‘74, 30-foot Pace Arrow motor home. The motor and transmission were still factory sealed.” While the 727 transmission and 440 bottom-end were still in great shape, the original cylinder heads were showing their age, so Ross replaced them with a set of heads from a Charger. The head swap also included a Lunati Thumpr cam, roller rockers, and an Edelbrock Torker intake topped with a 600-cfm carburetor. The 3.50:1 differential allows for a good compromise between acceleration and cruising, especially considering the big-block has a lot less mass to push around.


Ross found a ’32 grille shell and matched it with a set of ’32 commercial truck headlights. With the ’32 dash inside, his truck has got some of the best bits of a ’32 for a lower cost of entry. Besides that, Ross likes the details on the ‘34’s beltline.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


We asked how Ross was able to match the truck’s original paint to the new work. The process began with giving the bare metal a coat of etching primer, then red oxide primer, and topping it all with black paint. Using a red Scotch-Brite pad, he scuffed the paint to artificially age it. “It takes a little longer, but it gives it more of an aged look, and you don’t have the sanding marks in it,” Ross explained. After several trips to the Salt Flats, the truck had picked up a few bits of rust. He used alcohol to dissolve it and coax it out of the suspension before washing it with a grease-cutting dish soap. For the bare metal on the body that stood out because it *didn’t* rust, Ross mixed up a solution of alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, and rock salt to speed up oxidation. He then treated it to help it match the rest of the truck.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Ross and his wife Laura had wanted to go on a big road trip for the ages, and when they finally did so about seven years ago, they meandered through Tennessee and explored Nashville. Since they had the time, they decided to tour the Jack Daniel’s distillery in Lynchburg. They had so much fun that they decided to commemorate the trip by giving the truck a Jack Daniel’s theme, with some lettering on the door and the fuel tank. The tank is a repurposed beer keg in the bed next to the battery box that Ross fabricated and painted red with a Coca-Cola script. The Jack-and-Coke theme continues in the tempered safety glass that Ross had custom cut for the truck, which has a subtle tint of Coke-bottle green.


This Golden Spike marker from the US’s first transcontinental railroad represents a bit of home that travels with the truck wherever it goes.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The lace-painted roof was Laura’s idea. They already had a Halloween-themed tablecloth they’d used for decoration, so Ross sprayed the roof red with some metal flake and copper, stretched the lace over the top, and sprayed it black. It’s all coated in satin clear. Ross chose to go black over red rather than the reverse to keep things a bit more muted. The effect is barely noticeable from 10 feet away, especially during Speed Week when the truck is covered with a sprinkling of salt.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


With red wheels and a red lace roof, Laura thought the interior could use a bit of extra color and surprised Ross with the Moon Eyes steering wheel.


As with the paint, body, and mechanical labor, the interior was also Ross’s doing. He made a low-profile seat and covered it in a high-density, gel-infused foam. “It’s not very thick,” Ross admitted, “but it is very comfortable.” The low seats allow for more space in the chopped and channeled pickup. The floorboards are white oak, just like Jack Daniel’s barrels. “I’d always liked how the big rigs looked from the ’70s and early ’80s, how they had the stereo and everything overhead,” Ross said, noting his upholstered overhead console. With your eyes on the road, it’s just a quick glance up to check the gauges. “Plus, I didn’t want to cut that original factory ‘32 steel dash that my wife got for me.”


Ross’s wife, Laura, might have been on the fence about the pickup project at first, but quickly grew to appreciate it as it transformed. She also gifted Ross the Hy-Fire air cleaner that’s the crown jewel of the engine bay. “That was an old oil bath that I converted to a paper filter,” explained Ross.


Laura Kitman found the old DeSoto air cleaner a fitting, retro touch for the newer, bigger Mopar V8.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Along with the roof, the 16-inch Wheelsmith wheels got a splash of red.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Ross trailers the truck to Speed Week—he prefers to keep the small truck out of big rigs’ blind spots on the highway—but makes plenty of time to drive it around town and all over Utah. He and Laura use it weekly to grab a bite to eat, often breakfast on the weekends. “I’m not afraid to take it on the salt,” said Ross. “I build them to play with them.”


Ross Kitman
